newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Lithuania to talk currency, tariffs with IMF.
newsitem.headline: Lithuania to talk currency, tariffs with IMF.

text.p: Lithuania said on Thursday it plans to discuss the abolition of the currency board peg of its litas currency and import tariffs with an International Monetary Fund (IMF) mission next week.
Prime Minister Gediminas Vagnorius told a news conference he wanted the help of IMF experts to scrap the currency board.
The litas is pegged at four to one dollar under the board, which means an increase in local money supply has to backed by a proportional rise in hard currency reserves.
Lithuania wants to keep the peg but end the currency board, which strips the central bank of any monetary policy powers.
"I want to assure that there will be no abrupt changes and if there are any we will inform about them well in advance," Vagnorius said.
Under IMF agreements, the currency board has to be in place until at least September 1997.
The central bank last week unveiled its plans to end the currency board and take over running the fixed peg with money market tools and interest rate interventions.
The currency board has brought stability to the litas but some critics say it overvalues the currency and harms exports.
Vagnorius said the government would also discuss import tariffs with the IMF, as they were set at lower levels than under trade deals with European Union (EU) nations.
Under the IMF deal, Lithuania is requested to cut its average import tariffs to 20 percent by March.
Vagnorius did not say exactly what he wished to do about import tariffs but said current promises to the IMF were stricter than to EU nations.
"It looks strange when our obligations to the IMF are much stricter than to the countries we have free trade agreements with," Vagnorius added.

He said import tarriffs deserved special attention under a currency board model as prices for imported goods remained fixed for several years but production costs for local goods were rising due to inflation.
Vagnorius said Lithuania needed the means to protect its local market.
"Now it is hard to find a single product in Lithuania which is profitable to produce" he said.
